short: One slot of the HashMap's internal array. Every key whose index is that slot ends up in this bucket.
more: The JDK source calls it a "bin". A bucket holds nothing, one node, a chain of nodes, or a tree.

short: The internal array of buckets (Node<K,V>[] table). Its length is always a power of two.
more: Created lazily on the first put.

short: One key-value entry inside a bucket. Stores the key, the value, the key's hash and a pointer to the next node in the chain.
more: Roughly 32 bytes per entry on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers, not counting the key and value objects themselves.

short: A number computed from a key. HashMap uses it to decide which bucket the key belongs to.
more: Inside HashMap the "hash" is hashCode() after the high bits have been mixed in: h ^ (h >>> 16).

short: A method on every Java object that returns a 32-bit int summarising the object's contents. HashMap calls it on every key.
more: Equal objects must return equal hash codes. Different objects may share a hash code (a collision).

short: The method that decides whether two objects count as the same. HashMap calls it only after the hash codes match.
more: Default Object.equals compares identity (==). Override it together with hashCode.

short: The rules every hashCode()/equals() pair must obey, most importantly: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode().
more: Break it and a HashMap can "lose" entries it still holds.

short: Two different keys that land in the same bucket.
more: Unavoidable: there are about 4 billion possible hash codes but only a handful of buckets. HashMap resolves them by chaining.

short: Collision strategy where each bucket holds a linked list (a "chain") of all the entries that share it.
more: The alternative is open addressing, used by IdentityHashMap, where a colliding entry is placed in another free slot.

short: Collision strategy where a colliding entry is stored in some other free slot of the same array instead of in a list.
more: Used by IdentityHashMap in the JDK (linear probing).

short: A sequence of nodes where each node points to the next. Finding an item means walking from the front: O(n).
The number of buckets in the table (16 by default). Always a power of two; doubles on every resize.
The capacity you ask for in the constructor, e.g. new HashMap<>(64). HashMap rounds it up to the next power of two.
How full the table may get before it grows. Default 0.75: when size > capacity × 0.75, the table doubles.
more: Lower = fewer collisions but more memory. Higher = less memory but longer chains.

short: capacity × load factor. When the number of entries exceeds it, HashMap resizes. 12 for a 16-bucket table.
Doubling the table and moving entries into the new, larger array.
more: Java 8+ does not recompute any hash: each node either keeps its index or moves by exactly the old capacity.

short: Converting a long chain in one bucket into a red-black tree, so lookups drop from O(n) to O(log n).
more: Happens when a bucket reaches 9 nodes AND the table has at least 64 buckets. With fewer buckets HashMap resizes instead.

short: Turning a tree bucket back into a plain linked list when it has shrunk to 6 nodes or fewer.
A bucket that holds its nodes as a red-black tree (TreeNode objects) instead of a linked list.
more: TreeNodes are roughly twice as big as plain nodes, which is why HashMap only uses them for long chains.

short: A self-balancing binary search tree. Guarantees search, insert and delete in O(log n).
more: TreeMap is built on the same structure.

short: A tree where every node has at most two children, smaller keys on the left and larger on the right. Search takes one comparison per level.
The last-resort ordering inside a tree bin when hashes are equal and keys are not Comparable: class name, then identity hash code.
more: It keeps the tree consistent but cannot help lookups, which must then check both subtrees.

short: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 … Exactly one bit set in binary, which makes (n - 1) a mask of all ones.
more: That is why a bitwise AND can replace the slower modulo.

short: The & operator: each result bit is 1 only if both input bits are 1. With a mask like 0b1111 it keeps just the low bits.
The ^ operator: each result bit is 1 when the two input bits differ.
Unsigned right shift. h >>> 16 moves the top 16 bits down to the bottom and fills with zeros, even for negative numbers.
A number whose 1-bits select which bits of another number to keep when combined with &.
more: For capacity 16 the mask is 15 = 0b1111, so only the lowest 4 bits of the hash are used.

short: The % operator, the remainder after division. For a power-of-two n and non-negative h, h % n equals h & (n - 1) but the AND is faster and never negative.
HashMap's step h ^ (h >>> 16): it mixes the high 16 bits of the hash into the low 16 bits.
more: Only the low bits pick the bucket in a small table, so without this, hashes that differ only in high bits would all collide.

short: Constant time: the work does not grow with the number of entries.
Linear time: the work grows in step with the number of entries, e.g. walking a whole chain.
Logarithmic time: doubling the entries adds only one more step, as in a balanced tree.
Averaged over many operations. One resize is expensive, but spread over all the puts that led to it, the cost per put is still O(1).
An object whose fields can never change after construction (String, Integer, records). Ideal as map keys.
An object whose fields can change after construction. If a key's fields feed hashCode() and you change them, the map can no longer find it.
The default Object.hashCode(): a number tied to the object's identity, not its contents. Two equal-looking objects get different ones.
more: Not the memory address in modern JVMs; usually a generated pseudo-random number stored in the object header.

short: An interface with compareTo() that defines a natural order. Tree bins use it, when available, to order keys that share a hash.
more: String and Integer implement it.

short: A helper that combines several fields into one hash code (31 × previous + next field). Convenient for hashCode() implementations.
more: Allocates a varargs array, so hand-write the maths in very hot code.

short: A Java 16+ class for plain immutable data. The compiler generates equals(), hashCode() and toString() from the components.
more: Good map keys.

short: Automatic wrapping of a primitive such as int into its object type Integer, needed because maps hold objects.
Safe to use from several threads at once without corrupting data.
more: HashMap is not thread-safe.

short: A bug where the result depends on the unlucky timing of two threads touching the same data.
Two threads read the same value, both change it, and one change silently overwrites the other.
Java keyword that lets only one thread at a time run a block of code or method on a given lock.
A mechanism that lets only one thread at a time enter a critical section.
Compare-and-swap: a CPU instruction that updates a value only if it still holds the expected old value. Basis of lock-free algorithms.
more: ConcurrentHashMap uses it to put the first node into an empty bucket.

short: A thread-safe hash map. Java 8+: CAS for empty buckets, a lock on the first node of a bucket otherwise. No null keys or values.
more: Reads are lock-free; writes to different buckets run in parallel.

short: A legacy thread-safe map from Java 1.0. Every method is synchronized on one lock, and null keys/values are not allowed.
more: Avoid in new code.

short: Wraps any map so that every method takes a single lock. Thread-safe but a bottleneck under contention; iteration still needs manual locking.
An iterator that throws ConcurrentModificationException as soon as it notices the map was changed behind its back.
more: Best-effort only: it is a bug detector, not a guarantee.

short: Thrown by fail-fast iterators when the collection is structurally modified during iteration (other than via the iterator's own remove).
A counter HashMap increments on every structural change. Iterators remember it and compare it on each step to detect interference.
An object that walks through a collection one element at a time.
A HashMap that also keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order (or access order).
more: With accessOrder = true and removeEldestEntry it makes a simple LRU cache.

short: A map kept sorted by key, implemented as a red-black tree. O(log n) operations, no hashing.
more: Needs Comparable keys or a Comparator.

short: A set backed by a HashMap: the elements are the keys, and every value is the same dummy object.
A map that compares keys with == and System.identityHashCode instead of equals/hashCode. Used for object-graph work.
A map whose keys are held weakly: when nothing else references a key, the entry disappears.
A very compact map for enum keys, backed by an array indexed by the enum's ordinal.
Least-recently-used cache: when full, it evicts the entry that has gone unused the longest.
Map method that computes and stores a value only when the key is missing. The mapping function must not modify the same map.
A loop that never ends. In Java 7, concurrent resizes could turn a chain into a circle so a get() spun forever.
Memory that is still referenced and so can never be garbage-collected, though the program no longer uses it.
more: A mutated key can leave an unreachable-but-referenced entry in a map.

short: The JVM's automatic freeing of objects that nothing references any more.
The JVM memory area where objects live.
HashMap allows one null key; its hash is defined as 0, so it always lives in bucket 0.
Creating something only when first needed. HashMap allocates its table on the first put, not in the constructor.
Choosing the initial capacity from the expected number of entries, so the map never has to resize while filling.
more: Capacity needed = expected entries ÷ 0.75, rounded up.

short: A statistical model for how many random items land in one slot. The JDK authors used it to show that 8 nodes in a bucket is vanishingly rare with decent hash codes.
more: Chance of 8 nodes in one bucket is about 0.00000006.

short: Keys spread evenly across all buckets, which is what a good hash function aims for.
If you put more pigeons than holes, some hole must hold two. Here: more possible keys than buckets means collisions are certain.
A denial-of-service attack where someone sends many keys with the same hash code to force long chains and slow the server.
more: Tree bins (Java 8+) limit the damage to O(log n) when keys are Comparable.

short: An attack that makes a service too slow or busy to use.
One key-value pair of a Map, as seen through iteration. HashMap's Node implements it.
Java Development Kit: the compiler, tools and the standard library, including java.util.HashMap.
Java Virtual Machine, the runtime that executes Java bytecode.
A field modifier that makes writes visible to all threads immediately.
A counter that spreads updates over several cells to avoid contention. ConcurrentHashMap's size counter works the same way.
Whether one thread can see the changes made by another. Without synchronization it may not.
